items.title: L8: Interviewing when the panel knows you
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Code; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: Internal candidates often face a panel that includes someone they know, perhaps their own line manager or a colleague from another team. This creates two risks. The first is that you assume the panel already knows what you have done and skip the detail. Panels must score what they hear in the room, and a panel member cannot award marks for knowledge they hold privately, however well they know your work. Describe your examples in full, as if the panel has never met you, including the context and your own actions. The second risk is the opposite: acting stiffly or avoiding any reference to shared history. It is fine to say 'As you will know' and then give the detail anyway. If a panel member does know you well, departments normally expect them to declare it. Panels are expected to declare any close personal or working relationship that might affect fairness, and the recruitment team can then decide whether the panel needs changing. If you know a panel member personally, for example a family member or close friend, tell the recruitment team as soon as you learn who is on the panel; do not wait until the day. Under the Civil Service Recruitment Principles, selection must be on merit through fair and open competition, so a declared connection protects both you and the panel. Remember also that internal candidates are marked against the same criteria as external ones. Being in the department earns no bonus marks, and it does not excuse leaving out detail. Finally, avoid criticising colleagues or current managers when giving examples, because the panel may know them and it can reflect poorly on your judgement.

questions.prompt: Your line manager is on the interview panel. How should you approach an example about a project you both worked on?

options.text: Leave out the context but give the result in detail, as the manager knows the background
Describe it in full, including context and your own actions, as if they did not know
Summarise it in a sentence, since the panel member can fill in the detail when scoring
Keep it brief, because your manager already knows what you did and the panel can ask them

questions.hint: Panels can only score what they hear in the room.

questions.prompt: Why can a panel member not simply give credit for what they privately know of your work?

options.text: Scores must rest on the evidence given in the interview for all candidates alike
Panels may only credit examples drawn from the previous twelve months of work
Private knowledge is nearly always out of date by the time of the interview
The panel is not allowed to speak to line managers about a candidate's work history

questions.hint: Fairness requires the same basis for every candidate.

questions.prompt: Which phrasing is acceptable when a panel member knows the project?

options.text: 'You will remember what happened, so I will not repeat the details.'
'You can see from the project file what I did, so I won't go through it.'
'As you will know, we had a backlog; I'll explain what I did.'
'You were there, so I'll go straight to the result and skip the background.'

questions.hint: Acknowledging shared history is fine if you still give the evidence.

questions.prompt: You discover a close friend is on your interview panel. What is the best step?

options.text: Mention it only if the friend scores you lower than you expected
Say nothing, because a friendship will not affect how you answer the questions
Ask the friend to put in a good word for you with the other panel members
Tell the recruitment team as soon as you know, so they can decide what to do

questions.prompt: What do the Civil Service Recruitment Principles require of selection?

options.text: Selection by length of service in the department
Selection on merit following fair and open competition
Selection of existing staff ahead of outside applicants
Selection by recommendation from the hiring manager

questions.hint: Merit and open competition underpin fairness.

questions.prompt: Are internal candidates marked against different criteria from external ones?

options.text: They are given credit for time already in the department
They are marked on a reduced set of behaviours
They are marked against the same criteria for the role
They are marked only on their current job performance

questions.hint: The standard is the same for every candidate.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid criticising your current manager in an example?

options.text: Panels never ask about managers, so any mention of them would be irrelevant
Criticism is allowed about managers you no longer work for, but never current ones
Managers are rarely the cause of problems, so criticism is usually unfair
The panel may know them, and it can reflect poorly on your judgement

questions.hint: Respect and discretion show good judgement.

questions.prompt: Which risk is greatest for an internal candidate who assumes the panel 'just knows'?

options.text: Missing out the detail that earns marks
Giving answers that are too long
Mentioning the department by name
Appearing too confident to be liked

questions.prompt: A panel member says, 'You and I worked together, so I will be taking notes as normal.' What should you do?

options.text: Ask for a different panel member, since they already know too much about your work
Carry on and give full answers as you would to any panel member
Shorten your answers, because they already know the work you are describing
Treat it as a sign that you have already passed the stage they are scoring

questions.prompt: Which of these is a sign that panel members may need to be changed?

options.text: A panel member who has worked in the department for many years
A panel member who works in a different directorate from the vacancy
A panel member who has sat on several interview panels before
A close personal relationship with a candidate that has not been declared

items.title: L8: Political impartiality and current policy questions
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; GOV.UK
items.body: Civil servants serve the government of the day whatever its political party. The Civil Service Code's value of impartiality means carrying out your role with objectivity, and not allowing your own political views to influence your advice or actions. In an interview you might be asked about a current policy, a news story or a minister's decision. These questions are rarely about whether you agree. The panel wants to know whether you can discuss the issue fairly, understand the evidence on different sides and work professionally on policies you might privately disagree with. A strong answer shows understanding of what the policy aims to do, acknowledges that there are different views, and says that your role would be to provide accurate, evidence-based advice and to implement decisions lawfully. Avoid stating strong personal party-political opinions, praising or criticising named politicians, or suggesting that you would only work on policies you support. Equally, do not refuse to answer; saying 'I can't comment' sounds evasive. You can say 'My own views would not affect my work. What I can say is that the evidence suggests...'. Civil servants also face restrictions on political activity, with the most restrictive rules applying to more senior and sensitive posts, and the rules usually require permission or resignation for activities such as standing for election. If you are asked about your own political activity, answer honestly and factually. Finally, be careful with social media: your public posts can be read by colleagues and the public, and the Code applies to your conduct online as well as at work.

questions.prompt: What does impartiality in the Civil Service Code mean for how you advise?

options.text: Giving the minister the advice that you think they most want to hear
Advising only on the policies you personally support
Not letting your own political views shape your advice or actions
Never discussing government policy with anyone, in or outside of work

questions.prompt: A panel asks for your opinion on a current government policy. What is the panel mainly testing?

options.text: Whether you can discuss it fairly and work professionally regardless of your views
Whether you have campaigned about the policy in the past
Whether you agree with the political party currently in government
Whether you can recite the policy details from memory without notes

questions.prompt: Which answer best suits a question on a controversial policy?

options.text: Say you strongly disagree with it and set out your reasons in some detail to show conviction
Say the question is inappropriate for an interview and decline to answer it at all
Explain the aim, acknowledge differing views and say you would give evidence-based advice
Praise the minister and the party in government to show that you are loyal to them

questions.prompt: Why is 'I can't comment' a weak response?

options.text: Panels forbid short answers, so a refusal is marked as incomplete
It sounds evasive when you could discuss the issue without stating a party view
The Code requires you to give an opinion on every policy you are asked about
It suggests you have not heard of the policy being discussed

questions.hint: You can engage without taking sides.

questions.prompt: Which statement would raise concern about impartiality?

options.text: 'I would only work on policies I support.'
'I would give accurate advice even if the decision went against it.'
'I would explain the evidence for each option.'
'I would implement the decision lawfully.'

questions.hint: Civil servants serve the government of the day.

questions.prompt: Which is a sound way to separate your private views from your work?

options.text: 'I would keep my views to myself and ignore what the evidence says about it.'
'I would share my views with the minister's private office so they know where I stand.'
'I would argue publicly for my view if I disagreed with the decision.'
'My own views would not affect my work; what I can say is what the evidence shows.'

questions.hint: Evidence-based advice is the professional route.

questions.prompt: Who faces the most restrictive rules on political activity?

options.text: More senior and sensitive posts
Anyone who has applied for promotion
The newest recruits only
Staff who work outside London

questions.prompt: Standing for election while a civil servant usually requires what?

options.text: A vote among colleagues in your team to approve it
A letter to the press explaining your reasons for standing
Nothing at all, because it is a private matter outside work
Permission, or in some cases resignation, depending on the post

questions.hint: Rules vary by post and department.

questions.prompt: What should you do if asked about your own political activity at interview?

options.text: Deny any views you hold
Refuse, citing the Official Secrets Act
Answer honestly and factually
Exaggerate your involvement

questions.hint: Honesty applies everywhere in the Code.

questions.prompt: How does the Civil Service Code apply to what you post on social media?

options.text: It applies only to official channels used for departmental work
It applies to your conduct online as well as at work
It applies only when you post from a work device
It applies only to staff at senior grades

questions.hint: Your public posts reflect on the Civil Service.

items.title: L8: Hypothetical and situational questions
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs interview guidance
items.body: Besides past-example questions, panels may ask hypothetical ones: 'What would you do if...?'. They test your judgement and how you would apply the behaviours in a new situation. Because you have no real story to tell, structure becomes more important. A simple approach has five steps. First, clarify: state what you understand and, if needed, what you would check before acting. Second, identify the people affected and the priorities, such as service users, colleagues and deadlines. Third, set out the options and their risks. Fourth, choose an option and explain why, linking it to the role and to the Civil Service Code where relevant. Fifth, say how you would follow up, for example checking the result, informing your manager or recording what you did. Avoid answering with a single line such as 'I would ask my manager', which may be appropriate in part but shows no reasoning. Equally, do not claim you would solve everything alone: the panel expects you to know when to escalate and whom to involve. Do not describe an ideal world; deal with the constraint stated in the question, such as a short deadline or missing information. If the scenario depends on a fact you do not know, say what you would assume and why. When asked 'What would you do if you made a mistake?', the elements are to tell your manager promptly, correct what you can, learn and prevent repeats. If you can link the hypothetical to a real parallel from your experience, add one sentence, which makes the answer more credible.

questions.prompt: What is the first step in a good answer to a hypothetical question?

options.text: State your decision straight away so the panel knows you can act quickly
Clarify what you understand and what you would check before acting
Ask the panel to rephrase the question before you begin
Describe a real past example in place of the hypothetical one

questions.prompt: After clarifying, what should you identify?

options.text: Which answer the panel is most likely to prefer
Which option would be cheapest to carry out
Which colleague is most likely to be to blame for the problem
Who is affected and what the priorities are

questions.prompt: 'I would ask my manager.' Why is this a weak answer by itself?

options.text: It shows no reasoning about the options or what you would do first
It is too long to be scored fairly
Managers should never be asked for help with a problem like this
It does not mention the Civil Service Code

questions.hint: Escalation may be right but needs reasoning.

questions.prompt: Which answer shows poor judgement?

options.text: 'I would weigh up two options and pick the safer one.'
'I would check the facts and then tell my manager what I had found.'
'I'd deal with the whole situation alone so as not to trouble anyone.'
'I would explain the delay to the people affected as soon as I could.'

questions.hint: Knowing when to escalate is part of good judgement.

questions.prompt: The question gives a one-hour deadline. How should you answer?

options.text: Say it cannot be done in the time and leave it there
Ask the panel to move the deadline so that you can answer properly
Work within that constraint and say what you would prioritise
Ignore the constraint and describe how you would ideally approach it with more time

questions.prompt: What should you do if the scenario depends on a fact you do not know?

options.text: Choose the most dramatic assumption
Guess without saying so
Refuse to answer
State what you would assume and why

questions.prompt: 'What would you do if you made a mistake?' Which elements are expected?

options.text: Blame the system if it allowed the error to happen
Tell your manager promptly, correct what you can, and prevent a repeat
Wait and see whether anyone notices before deciding what to do
Correct it quietly yourself and say nothing to anyone else

questions.prompt: Why add a real parallel from your experience to a hypothetical answer?

options.text: It makes the answer more credible by showing you have done something similar
It counts as a second answer and earns a second score
It means that the panel will not ask any further questions
It lets you avoid explaining your reasoning in the hypothetical

questions.prompt: What is the final step in the five-step approach?

options.text: Ask the panel whether your answer was the one they wanted
Say how you would follow up or check the result
Summarise the question again in your own words
Apologise for any shortcomings in what you have just said

questions.prompt: Which Code value is most relevant when a scenario involves incomplete evidence?

options.text: Generosity
Speed
Loyalty
Objectivity

items.title: L8: Mapping one story to several behaviours
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Behaviours; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: A single strong example can contain evidence for more than one behaviour. A project to cut the time to process applications might show Changing and Improving (spotting a better way), Communicating and Influencing (persuading colleagues to adopt it), Working Together (agreeing it with other teams) and Managing a Quality Service (checking errors did not rise). Mapping your stories to behaviours before the interview helps you choose the right angle for each question. The method is to list the actions in your story, then note which behaviour each one demonstrates. In the interview you then emphasise only the actions that match the question. If asked about Communicating and Influencing, you describe how you made the case, anticipated objections and checked understanding; you mention the process improvement only as context. If asked about Changing and Improving, you reverse the emphasis. This keeps your answers distinct even if the story is the same. It also helps to hold some stories in reserve. Panels often score each behaviour independently and look for evidence in each answer, so reusing a story is best avoided if you have enough material. Aim for three to five strong stories for an EO interview, each mapped to two or three behaviours, plus a few smaller examples. Do not force a story into a behaviour it does not show: a story about working alone rarely demonstrates Working Together. Finally, check the grade. A story that shows initiative at AO level may not show enough scope for HEO, so mapping also means checking the level of responsibility.

questions.prompt: A project to cut processing time could provide evidence for which combination of behaviours?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture and Leadership, because they both show vision and direction
Delivering at Pace only, because the project saved a good deal of time
Changing and Improving, Communicating and Influencing, and Managing a Quality Service
Leadership only, because you introduced the change for the whole team

questions.hint: One story can show several behaviours.

questions.prompt: What is the first step in mapping a story?

options.text: List the actions in the story
Choose the longest example
Write out the story word for word
Decide which behaviour you like best

questions.prompt: You are asked about Communicating and Influencing for a process improvement story. What should you emphasise?

options.text: The manager who approved the change and what they said
The technical details of how the new process worked from day to day
How you made the case, anticipated objections and checked understanding
The amount of time that the new process saved the team

questions.hint: Match emphasis to the behaviour asked.

questions.prompt: The same story is used for Changing and Improving. What changes?

options.text: You emphasise spotting the problem and designing the better way
The story is told in the same way, but with a different opening line
You drop the result so the focus stays on the idea
You describe the persuasion of colleagues in the greatest detail

questions.prompt: Why is it still wise to avoid reusing a story if you have enough material?

options.text: Reuse of stories is against the interview rules
Panels score each behaviour independently and want evidence for each
It makes the interview take longer than the time allowed
Panels dislike hearing the same words used more than once

questions.prompt: How many strong stories is sensible for an EO interview?

options.text: None, since improvising is always more natural
Fifteen, so that every possible question is covered
One, as a single strong story can answer every question
Three to five, each mapped to two or three behaviours

questions.prompt: Why should you not force a story into a behaviour?

options.text: The panel will ask you for a different story as soon as they notice
It uses too much of the time you have available
Panels do not mark stories that have been adapted
It will not contain evidence of that behaviour

questions.hint: A story about working alone rarely shows Working Together.

questions.prompt: Which story would map best to Working Together?

options.text: Agreeing a shared process with another team that had different priorities
Fixing a recurring fault on the office printer without asking for help
Reading and summarising a long policy document for your own use
Completing a long report alone at home to a very tight deadline

questions.prompt: What else should you check when mapping a story?

options.text: That your manager appears in it
That the story is at least ten years old
That the responsibility level matches the grade
That it has no figures

questions.prompt: Why keep a few small examples in reserve?

options.text: They avoid the need to describe a result
They help when a question does not fit your main stories
They can replace your main stories when you want a change
They can be used for every question to save preparation

items.title: L8: Staying composed after a poor answer
items.source: Civil Service Jobs interview guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Almost every candidate gives at least one answer they regret. The skill is to stop that answer from affecting the rest of the interview. Panels score question by question, so a weak answer to one behaviour does not decide your result. Scores are added up, and a strong set of other answers can make up for it. Recognise what happens physically: your pulse rises, you may rush, and you may keep replaying the last answer instead of listening to the next question. Use a reset routine: take a slow breath, relax your shoulders, take a sip of water, and listen to the whole of the next question before answering. Do not apologise repeatedly or comment on how badly you think you did; it distracts the panel and wastes time. If you realise you left out a key point, you can add a short sentence at the end of that answer or, later, if offered the chance to add anything. If you blank on a question, it is acceptable to say 'Can I take a moment to think?' and pause for several seconds, which often feels longer to you than to the panel. If nothing comes, say honestly that you cannot think of an example straight away and ask to come back to it. Panels often allow this. If you do not return to it, move on calmly. After the interview, resist judging yourself by how you felt: candidates are often poor judges of their performance, and nerves make answers feel worse than they sounded.

questions.prompt: Why does one weak answer not decide the result?

options.text: Scores are given question by question and added up
Only the last answer given in the interview counts for the score
A weak answer is deleted from the record if you give a good one after
Panels ignore the first answer in every behaviour round

questions.prompt: What is a sensible reset after a poor answer?

options.text: Ask the panel how the last answer was going before you carry on
Speed up your next answer to make up for the time that was lost
A slow breath, relaxed shoulders and listening to the whole next question
Apologise for the last answer before you begin the next one

questions.prompt: Why is repeated apologising unhelpful?

options.text: It is only allowed once in each interview
It distracts the panel and wastes time
The Code forbids apologies of any kind to a panel
It signals that you want to leave the interview

questions.hint: Move on after a short acknowledgement.

questions.prompt: You left out a key point. When can you add it?

options.text: Never, because once an answer is finished it cannot be changed in any way
In an email sent to the recruitment team after the interview has finished
During any later answer, in full, as if it were a new point altogether
As a short sentence at the end of that answer, or when offered the chance to add anything

questions.prompt: You blank on a question. What is a good first response?

options.text: Ask for a moment to think, and pause for a few seconds
Start talking and hope that something useful emerges
Ask the panel to give you an example to work from
Say you cannot answer and move on to the next question at once

questions.prompt: No example comes to mind after a pause. What is sensible?

options.text: Make up an example that sounds close to what is being asked
Say the question is unfair and decline to answer it
Say you cannot think of one straight away and ask to come back to it
Describe a hypothetical case without telling the panel it is one

questions.prompt: You do not return to the question you skipped. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the panel to stop the interview
Apologise at the end
Try to answer it during another question
Move on calmly

questions.hint: Do not let it unsettle the rest.

questions.prompt: Why are candidates poor judges of their own performance?

options.text: Candidates usually talk too quickly to follow their own answers
Nerves make answers feel worse than they sounded
Candidates tend to remember too little of what they said
Panels hide the scores until months after the interview

questions.prompt: What physical effect often leads to rushed answers?

options.text: Sitting in a chair
Looking at the camera
Eating before the interview
A raised pulse from nerves

questions.prompt: After an interview you feel you did badly. What is the best approach?

options.text: Withdraw your application before the outcome is announced
Email the panel to apologise for the answers you regret
Wait for the outcome rather than judging yourself by how you felt
Ask the panel to rescore the answers you were unhappy with

questions.hint: You cannot know how it scored.

items.title: L8: Recorded and one-way video interviews
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance on assessment methods; GOV.UK
items.body: Some Civil Service recruitment uses pre-recorded video responses as an early stage, instead of a live panel. You receive a link, read or hear a question and record your answer within a set time, with limits on preparation and the number of attempts. Details differ by competition, so read the instructions carefully: how many questions, how long to prepare, how long to answer, whether you can re-record, and the deadline. The questions are usually behaviour or strengths questions like those in live interviews, and answers are scored against the same criteria, often by assessors who watch later. Preparation matters even more because there is no panel to prompt you. Practise answering aloud to a timer, aiming for a clear structure and finishing a little under the limit. Test your camera, microphone and connection beforehand, choose a quiet, well-lit room and place the camera at eye level. Look at the lens rather than the screen. You cannot see reactions, so speak with energy and finish properly rather than trailing off. If re-recording is allowed, use it sparingly: repeated attempts can produce more stilted answers. If you have a disability or need adjustments such as extra time, request them before you begin, because it may be difficult to arrange once the session has started. If a technical failure occurs, contact the recruitment team straight away with a description and, if possible, a screenshot. Treat the recorded answer as you would a live one: it is your evidence, so include the action and the result.

questions.prompt: What should you read first when given a one-way video interview link?

options.text: The instructions on questions, timings, attempts and deadline
Nothing in advance, because the instructions appear on screen later
The answers that other candidates have recorded for practice
The questions only, since the rest is the same for every competition

questions.prompt: Why does preparation matter even more for a recorded interview?

options.text: The recording will be much longer than a live answer
There is no panel to prompt or guide you
The panel will score the recording more quickly and less carefully
The questions are always harder than those in a live interview

questions.hint: You must structure the answer yourself.

questions.prompt: Which way of practising for a recorded answer is most useful?

options.text: Practising only on the day itself so that it sounds fresh
Answering aloud to a timer and finishing slightly under the limit
Writing a full script and reading it aloud to the camera
Reading your prepared answers silently to save time

questions.prompt: Where should the camera be placed?

options.text: Below your chin, so that the panel sees your notes on the desk
Beside a busy door, so that colleagues can find you if needed
Behind a bright window, so that the room looks light and open
At eye level, in a quiet, well-lit room

questions.prompt: Where should you look when recording?

options.text: At the camera lens
At your notes
At the ceiling
At your own image on screen

questions.prompt: If re-recording is allowed, how should it be used?

options.text: Repeatedly, until you feel the recording is perfect
For every question, to give yourself the best chance
Sparingly, since many attempts can produce stilted answers
Never, because only the first attempt is scored

questions.prompt: When should you request adjustments for a recorded interview?

options.text: After you submit
Before you begin
Only after the result
After the first question

questions.prompt: A technical failure occurs. What should you do?

options.text: Contact the recruitment team straight away with a description
Wait until the deadline has passed and then explain what happened
Re-record without telling anyone so that nobody knows
Post about the failure publicly so that others can help

questions.prompt: Who usually scores recorded answers?

options.text: An automatic system that checks spelling
The candidate's own line manager
The candidate, who reviews and scores their own answers
Assessors who watch later, against the same criteria

questions.hint: Criteria are the same as live interviews.

questions.prompt: What should a recorded answer still include?

options.text: Only your opinions
Only the situation
The action and the result
A summary of the job advert

items.title: L8: Declaring interests and resolving conflicts
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; Civil Service Recruitment Principles
items.body: A conflict of interest arises when a personal interest could, or could appear to, influence your official duties. In recruitment, it can affect panel members and candidates. For candidates, common situations include a relative or close friend working in the team you are applying to join, a past business relationship with the department, or a second job that overlaps with the role. If you know any of these, declare them to the recruitment team early. It does not usually stop you applying; it lets the department manage the risk, for example by keeping you out of any decision involving that person. For panel members, the principle is the same. They are expected to declare relationships with candidates, and a panel member who is related to or closely connected with a candidate would normally stand down from assessing that person. In a behaviour question you may also be asked about a conflict of interest, for example: 'Tell us about a time you had to deal with a conflict of interest'. A strong answer identifies the interest, shows you disclosed it to your manager promptly rather than hoping nobody noticed, explains how it was managed, and shows that the outcome was fair. Accepting gifts or hospitality that might appear to influence you, and failing to declare outside work, are other typical issues. The Code's integrity value includes not misusing your position for personal gain. The key message is transparency: declaring an interest is not an admission of wrongdoing, but hiding one can become a serious breach.

questions.prompt: What is a conflict of interest?

options.text: A difference of opinion with your manager about which work has priority
Two job offers received at the same time from different departments
A disagreement between two colleagues about how some work should be done
A personal interest that could, or could appear to, influence your official duties

questions.hint: It includes the appearance of influence.

questions.prompt: A candidate's cousin works in the team they have applied to. What should they do?

options.text: Say nothing unless someone asks you about it directly
Declare it to the recruitment team early
Ask the cousin to help you prepare for the interview
Withdraw immediately from the competition

questions.prompt: Does declaring an interest usually stop you applying?

options.text: Not usually; it lets the department manage the risk
Only if the person is a manager in the team
Always, because the department cannot manage the risk
Only for senior posts, where the risk is greater

questions.prompt: A panel member is related to a candidate. What is expected?

options.text: The panel member scores the candidate higher to compensate for the connection
The candidate is rejected from the competition automatically as a precaution
The panel member declares it and normally stands down from assessing that candidate
Nothing needs to change, provided the panel member gives a fair score

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest answer to 'Tell us about a conflict of interest you dealt with'?

options.text: I asked a colleague to take over the work without explaining the reason why
I decided myself that the interest was small, so I carried on without mentioning it
I kept it private to avoid any fuss and made sure my work was not affected
I recognised the interest, told my manager promptly, and we agreed how to manage it so the outcome was fair

questions.prompt: Which situation is a typical conflict of interest for a civil servant?

options.text: Eating lunch at your desk instead of in the canteen
Awarding a contract to a firm owned by a relative
Working flexible hours agreed with your manager
Attending a training course run by an outside provider

questions.hint: Personal gain or connection with a decision.

questions.prompt: Which Code value does misusing your position for personal gain breach?

options.text: Integrity
Teamwork
Speed
Impartiality only

questions.hint: Integrity includes not misusing your position.

questions.prompt: Why is hiding an interest worse than declaring it?

options.text: Declaring is a duty for managers only, so other staff need not do it
Hiding an interest is normal and is never treated as a breach of the Code
Concealment can become a serious breach, while declaring is not an admission of wrongdoing
Declaring leads to automatic dismissal, so concealment is the safer route in practice

questions.prompt: A candidate has a second job that overlaps with the role. What should they do?

options.text: Leave the second job quietly without telling the department
Tell no one, because it is a private matter
Hide it until after an offer has been made
Declare it so that the department can assess whether it is compatible

questions.prompt: Gifts that might appear to influence you should be treated how?

options.text: Shared out among the team without telling anyone
Declined or declared, in line with department rules
Accepted if they are small, whatever the circumstances
Kept secret to avoid awkward questions

items.title: L8: Negotiating and weighing up an offer
items.body: A Civil Service job offer normally states the grade, salary, location, working pattern and start date, and is subject to checks. Pay in the Civil Service is set through pay ranges for each grade, which differ between departments. New starters usually begin at or near the bottom of the range for the grade, and departments often have limited flexibility to start people higher. Where flexibility exists it is usually tied to recruitment and retention needs, and requires approval, so do not assume any negotiation will succeed. You can ask politely whether the salary is fixed, and explain relevant experience, but be realistic. Think about the whole package: pension, leave, flexible working, learning opportunities, location and career progression, not just salary. The Civil Service pension is a significant part of the reward, and annual leave is often generous. If you have more than one offer, compare them on pay, role content, development, location and security of the post. Ask for any answers you need in writing, such as hybrid working expectations or whether the post is permanent or fixed term. Acceptance letters are usually simple, but they confirm your agreement, so read them carefully before replying. If you decide to decline, do so promptly and politely so the department can offer the post to the next candidate on the reserve list. Never accept a post you do not intend to take up. Avoid resigning from your existing job until the conditions of your offer are met and you have a written confirmation.

items.title: L8: Analysing a full answer for strengths and gaps
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles guidance; Civil Service Jobs interview guidance
items.body: Practising with a recording helps you judge your own answers as a panel would. Take a typical answer: 'In my last job we had a lot of complaints about delays. As a team we looked at the process, and I think we improved it. It took a few weeks but things got better and the manager was happy.' To evaluate it, use four lenses. First, behaviour match: if the question was Managing a Quality Service, the story is relevant, but the answer does not state the standard or the quality measure. Second, personal action: 'we looked at the process' and 'I think we improved it' give no sign of what the candidate did. Third, specificity: 'a lot', 'a few weeks' and 'things got better' are vague, so a panel cannot tell the scale or the change. Fourth, reasoning and learning: there is no explanation of why the approach was chosen or what the candidate learned. A stronger version would say: 'We received around forty complaints a month about delays. I analysed three months of cases and found that most delays happened at one approval step. I proposed a two-day limit and drafted a simple checklist; I agreed it with the team leader and trialled it for a month. Complaints fell to about fifteen.' Notice that the improved answer is not much longer; it simply replaces generalities with actions and numbers. When you review your own recording, count how many times you say 'I' with a verb, how many specific facts you give, and whether you state a result. A useful rule is that every answer should contain at least two named actions and one measurable change.

questions.prompt: In the sample answer, what does 'As a team we looked at the process' show?

options.text: A strong personal action that earns high marks
A good result with evidence behind it
Nothing about what the candidate personally did
A clear measure of the quality of the service

questions.prompt: Which lens asks whether the story fits the question?

questions.hint: The improved answer is not much longer.

options.text: It uses fewer words overall

items.title: L8: Dealing with a hostile or sceptical panel member
items.source: Civil Service Jobs interview guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Occasionally a panel member seems sceptical or blunt. They might say 'That doesn't sound very impressive' or 'Surely that was your manager's job?'. Most of the time it is deliberate: panels are trained to probe and to test how you respond to challenge. Behaviours such as Communicating and Influencing and Making Effective Decisions expect you to handle disagreement calmly. The best response has three parts. First, stay neutral: keep your tone steady and avoid defensiveness. Second, acknowledge the point where it is fair: 'That's a fair challenge; the decision was my manager's, but I prepared the options'. Third, give evidence: restate the fact or action that answers the doubt. Avoid arguing, sulking or over-explaining. If you realise you made a mistake or overstated something, correct it briefly, which shows honesty. Do not let the scepticism of one panel member influence how you speak to the others; maintain eye contact with all of them. If a question seems unfair or discriminatory, stay polite, say you would prefer to focus on the role, and raise the concern afterwards with the recruitment team. If a panel member is rude or aggressive beyond normal challenge, you may say calmly that you are finding it difficult to continue, and ask for a short break; most panels will respond appropriately. Afterwards, report the behaviour to the recruitment team in writing, factually. In most cases, however, scepticism is part of fair, structured assessment and is not personal. A calm, evidence-based reply often scores well precisely because it shows resilience.

questions.prompt: A panel member says 'Surely that was your manager's job?' What is the best response?

options.text: Insist that it was entirely your job and say no more
Say that the panel member has misunderstood the role
Acknowledge the fair point and then explain what you did to contribute

items.title: L8: Preparing a development plan from feedback
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs recruitment guidance
items.body: After an unsuccessful or borderline interview, feedback is valuable only if you turn it into a plan. Begin by collecting the information: scores or comments for each behaviour, your own notes of the questions and what you said, and any recording. Look for patterns. If the same weakness appears across questions, such as vague results or hidden personal actions, that is a habit to fix. If one behaviour scored low but others were fine, you may have chosen a poor example or lacked experience in that area. Decide which type of gap you have. A technique gap, such as weak structure or no result, can be fixed through practice within weeks. A content gap, such as little evidence of Leadership, needs new experience: volunteering, project work, covering for a manager, mentoring or taking on a coordinating role. Set specific, short-term goals, such as 'rewrite my five examples with a numerical result', or 'run a mock interview each fortnight'. Ask someone to listen and give feedback; ideally someone who knows the Success Profiles. Record yourself and compare. Keep an evidence log: each month, write down one achievement with the action and result, so you build examples over time rather than trying to remember them for the next application. Finally, review the plan before the next application and adjust. It is also reasonable to apply for a different grade or role if the feedback suggests it, or to look for a development opportunity, such as a secondment or learning programme in your department, which can strengthen your evidence in a way that practice alone cannot.

items.title: L8: Spoken style: filler, jargon and acronyms
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Communicating and Influencing; GOV.UK writing guidance
items.body: Spoken answers are judged on clarity as well as content. Three habits commonly weaken them. The first is filler: repeated 'um', 'you know', 'basically' and 'like'. A few are natural, and panels do not mark them down heavily, but constant filler hides the point and can suggest you are unprepared. Replace filler with a short silent pause; pausing sounds more confident than it feels. The second is jargon and acronyms. Civil Service departments use many abbreviations, but panel members may come from other departments or from outside, and an acronym that is routine in your team may mean nothing to them. Say the full term the first time, for example 'the quarterly management report', and use plain words for processes. GOV.UK writing guidance recommends plain English for the same reason: it helps readers understand quickly. The third is hedging: starting every sentence with 'I just', 'I sort of' or 'I think maybe', which dilutes ownership. State your actions directly: 'I drafted the checklist'. This is different from honest uncertainty about facts, where saying 'I think it was about thirty' is appropriate. Pace matters too. Speaking too fast under nerves makes answers hard to follow; aim for a steady rhythm, with a pause at the end of each main point. Finally, remember that clear, short sentences are easier for note-taking panel members to capture accurately, which helps your score.
